source.title_on_document: Empower or Disempower: The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on College Students' Creativity

supplement.where: None. The paper refers to no supplementary material, online appendix, data, or code.
supplement.holds: Not applicable. Every statistic is in the main text (Sections II.B and III) and in Tables I and II (PDF pp. 3-4, printed pp. 663-664).

paper_design_summary: After a baseline brick Alternative Uses Test, undergraduates at one university in Gansu Province, China, were randomly assigned to draw an alien for 10 minutes with the Kimi.AI web interface available or without GAI. The study analyzed 113 people (58 with Kimi.AI, 55 without GAI); the arms were tested separately. Two independent coders rated overall creativity, similarity to Earth creatures, and atypical features, and the paper compared the groups using independent-samples t-tests (PDF pp. 2-4, Sections II.A-II.C and III.B, Tables I-II).

studies.label: Lab experiment: draw an alien with or without Kimi.AI

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of the generative AI tool Kimi.AI (web interface pre-opened in a computer-equipped laboratory) versus no GAI tool during the 10-minute alien-drawing task
assignment.quote: Next, the participants were randomly assigned to either the group using GAI tools or the group not using such tools.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 663), Section II.B Experimental Procedure; the design is called single-factor between-subjects at PDF p. 2 (printed p. 662), Section II.B

arms.name: GAI group (experimental group; Table II 'Yes')
arms.description: Drew the alien for 10 minutes in a computer-equipped laboratory with the Kimi.AI web interface pre-opened, after a brief introduction on how to operate it.

arms.name: No-GAI group (control group; Table II 'No')
arms.description: Completed the same 10-minute alien-drawing task independently, without GAI tools.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper says 113 students were recruited and that the participants were randomly assigned. Table I, which each group filled in after assignment and before the task, gives 58 and 55, and its gender rows (27 + 28 male, 31 + 27 female) match the 55 males and 58 females recruited. Table II reports every outcome for Yes N=(58) and No N=(55). The paper gives no separate count at the moment of assignment, so the randomized counts rest on Table I.
participants.who: Undergraduate students from a comprehensive university in Gansu Province; mean age 19.71 (SD 0.89); 55 male, 58 female
participants.quote: A total of 113 college students were recruited for the experiment, with an average age of 19.71 years (standard deviation = 0.89), including 55 males and 58 females.
participants.locator: PDF p. 2 (printed p. 662), Section II.A Study Design; PDF p. 3 (printed p. 663), Section II.B and Table I (N=58/55); PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Table II

ai_tool.name_model: Kimi.AI (the paper calls it 'the generative AI tool Kimi AI'; web interface; model version not stated)
ai_tool.how_used: The Kimi.AI web interface was pre-opened on the laboratory computers, with a brief introduction on how to operate it, and was available during the 10-minute drawing task. The paper does not describe what participants asked the tool, whether it produced images, or whether the drawing was made on paper or on screen.

task.description: Structured imagination task adapted from Maddux and Galinsky (2009): imagine traveling to another galaxy, visiting a planet very different from Earth but inhabited by aliens, and draw a picture of the aliens living on this planet.

outcomes.name: Overall creativity of the alien drawing (Table II: Total Creativity)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two independent coders, unrelated to the experiment, rated each drawing on a 7-point scale (1 = not creative at all, 7 = highly creative); ICC = 0.87; the two coders' scores were averaged. The paper does not state the coders' expertise.

contrasts.reported: Table II, Total Creativity: Yes N=(58) M 6.03, SD 0.90; No N=(55) M 4.71, SD 1.34. Text: t (113) = 6.20, p = 0.002, d = 1.16. The text attributes both means to 'the unused group' ('The unused group novelty score was higher (M = 6.03, SD = 0.90) than in the unused group (M = 4.71, SD = 1.34).'); Table II assigns 6.03 to the GAI (Yes) group.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Section III.B Creativity and Table II

outcomes.name: Similarity of the alien drawing to Earth creatures (Table II: Similarity to Terrestrial Life)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two independent coders; two items (similarity to humans, similarity to other Earth animals), recorded on a 7-point scale; ICC = 0.63; the coders' scores were averaged. The paper does not specify how the two items were combined; Table II reports arm means of 12.87 and 10.90, which exceed 7. Higher scores indicate greater similarity to Earth creatures. The paper does not specify how this direction maps to creativity or novelty, so no creativity sign reversal is coded. This is similarity to a reference, not similarity across participants' outputs (PDF p. 3, printed p. 663, Section II.C; PDF p. 4, printed p. 664, Section III.B and Table II).

contrasts.reported: Table II, Similarity to Terrestrial Life: Yes N=(58) M 12.87, SD 0.75; No N=(55) M 10.90, SD 1.23. Text: t (113) = 10.33, p <0.001, d = 1.93. The text attributes both means to 'the unused group' ('The earth biological similarity in the unused group (M =12.87, SD = 0.75) was higher than in the unused group (M = 10.90, SD = 1.23).'); Table II assigns 12.87 to the GAI (Yes) group. Direction is on the similarity score as printed: the GAI group's drawings were rated more similar to Earth creatures. The paper does not specify a creativity or novelty direction for this score.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Section III.B Creativity and Table II

outcomes.name: Atypical features of the alien drawing (Table II: Atypical Characteristics)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two coders; five items on sensory organs and body characteristics (absence of sensory organs or body parts, unusual quantities, uncommon shapes, unusual functions, special abilities); ICC = 0.91; the coders' scores were averaged. The paper gives no response scale for these items. A higher score means more atypical: the text calls the GAI group's higher mean 'more atypical'.

contrasts.reported: Table II, Atypical Characteristics: Yes N=(58) M 3.68, SD 1.03; No N=(55) M 2.08, SD 0.77. Text: t (113) = 9.27, p = 0.005 and d = 1.76; 'It was more atypical (M = 3.68, SD = 1.03) than the unused group (M = 2.08, SD = 0.77).'
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Section III.B Creativity and Table II

company_involvement.description: None stated. Kimi.AI is the tool tested, and the paper names no role for its developer. Funding: Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities (31920250129).

eligibility.reason: The paper explicitly states that participants were randomly assigned to Kimi.AI access or no GAI during the alien-drawing task (PDF p. 3, printed p. 663, Section II.B). It analyzed 113 people, with 58 in the GAI arm and 55 in the no-GAI arm (PDF p. 4, printed p. 664, Table II). Two independent coders scored the participants' drawings, including overall creativity and atypical features (PDF p. 3, printed p. 663, Section II.C), so all three criteria are met in S1. S1-O2 is retained as other because the paper does not map similarity to Earth creatures onto a creativity or novelty direction. Randomization implementation remains open for author clarification: the procedure is unspecified, the arms were tested separately, and only the GAI arm is specifically described as being in a computer-equipped laboratory (PDF pp. 2-3, Sections II.A-II.B). Table I lists 0 experimental versus 8 control participants aged 18 (PDF p. 3); this imbalance warrants clarification but does not contradict the explicit random-assignment statement. The printed statistical inconsistencies affect extraction and interpretation rather than the three screening criteria (see open_questions).

one_line_finding: Students randomly assigned to draw an alien with Kimi.AI available scored higher than students without AI on rated overall creativity (6.03 vs 4.71 on a 7-point scale; t (113) = 6.20, p = 0.002, d = 1.16) and atypical features (3.68 vs 2.08; d = 1.76), but also higher on similarity to Earth creatures (12.87 vs 10.90; d = 1.93) (PDF p. 4, printed p. 664, Section III.B and Table II).
open_questions: Randomization and testing sessions: participants are explicitly described as randomly assigned, but the allocation procedure is not given (PDF p. 3, printed p. 663, Section II.B). The arms were tested separately (PDF p. 2, printed p. 662, Section II.A), and the paper gives neither session counts nor a specific description of the no-GAI arm's room; only the GAI arm is described as placed in a computer-equipped laboratory (PDF p. 3, Section II.B). Table I also lists all participants aged 18 in the control arm (0 experimental, 8 control; PDF p. 3). Allocation and session details bear on verification of criterion 1, which is met on the paper's explicit statement; the source does not establish different rooms or disprove random assignment.

Arm-label errors: the creativity and similarity results text calls both groups the unused group, whereas Table II labels the 58-person rows Yes and the 55-person rows No under Whether to Use AIG. The form follows those table labels; Table I also identifies the 58-person arm as experimental. Corrected prose or author confirmation would settle the wording discrepancy (PDF p. 3, Table I; PDF p. 4, Section III.B and Table II).

Similarity direction and scoring rules: Section II.C defines similarity to humans and other Earth animals but does not say whether greater similarity is more or less creative. S1-O2 is therefore coded other, with no inferred novelty loss or sign reversal. The reported means (12.87 and 10.90) exceed the stated 7-point item scale, but the item-aggregation rule is unspecified; the response scale for the five atypical-feature items is also unspecified (PDF p. 3, Section II.C; PDF p. 4, Table II). Author clarification of the rubric would settle these measurement questions; rated overall creativity independently meets criterion 3.

Printed statistics: every two-group test is printed as t (113), using the same number as the reported sample size, and several printed p-values are inconsistent with the printed t statistics. Examples are creativity t (113) = 6.20, p = 0.002 and atypicality t (113) = 9.27, p = 0.005 (PDF p. 4, Section III.B); baseline AUT originality t(113) = 4.09, p = 0.06 and flexibility t(113) = 3.87, p = 0.26 (PDF pp. 2-3, Section II.B). Enjoyment is printed as t (113) = 1.21.22 (PDF p. 3, Section III.A). The paper does not establish which values require correction. The form preserves the printed Table II counts, means and SDs and the printed tests; corrected results or underlying data from the authors would settle the inconsistencies.

Intervention details: the GAI group performed the task on a pre-opened Kimi.AI web interface, but the prompts, generated content, and method of making the final drawing are not described. It is unclear whether participants requested ideas or images and whether the drawing was made on paper or on screen (PDF pp. 2-3, Sections II.A-II.B). These details would refine the intervention description; the source already specifies access to generative AI and scoring of participants' drawings.

Table I reporting: prior-AI-experience counts differ between arms (Daily: 3 experimental versus 13 control). The control-column experience entries sum to 65, whereas the table heading and its gender and age counts identify 55 control participants; the experimental experience entries sum to 58. The label I have used it several times, but I do not use it regularly spans rows with two numeric pairs (13/15 and 15/12), leaving a category label unclear. No balance test for Table I is reported. Corrected experience categories and counts require author clarification; participant totals are supported separately by Tables I and II (PDF p. 3, Table I; PDF p. 4, Table II).

Baseline AUT raters: the scoring text names two psychology experts but says the final originality score is the average of the three raters' scores (PDF p. 3, printed p. 663, Section II.C). Author clarification would settle the rater count. This concerns the baseline AUT before AI assignment and does not affect the drawing outcomes or eligibility.
notes: PDF pages 1-5 are printed pages 661-665. The brick Alternative Uses Test (fluency, originality, flexibility; five-minute limit; scored by two psychology experts) was given before random assignment as a balance check. It is not an AI-affected outcome and is not listed. The paper prints only t and p for it: originality t(113) = 4.09, p = 0.06; fluency t(113) = 0.27, p = 0.17; flexibility t(113) = 3.87, p = 0.26 (PDF pp. 2-3), with no arm means. Post-task familiarity, enjoyment, and motivation (7-point Likert; Table II) are self-reported control variables, not outcomes scored on the output. No diversity outcome is reported. The analysis is participant-level independent-samples t-tests, and no standard errors are printed. Primary status: the design names 'the creativity score' as the dependent variable, so S1-O1 is paper_primary and S1-O2 and S1-O3 are secondary (see reconciliation). The search record's leads are resolved: the paper states random assignment, and the 113 are people. Final source check: the full markdown was read through the references; the five-page PDF contains no appendix and refers to no supplement. Participant counts and the recorded outcome statistics were checked against the PDF text and Tables I-II. The final correction codes similarity to Earth creatures as other and retains the printed similarity direction without inferring a novelty loss. All reconciliation differences were already marked resolved; the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the earlier audit record.

differences.resolved: paper_primary (A). The design section names one dependent variable, the creativity score of the drawing, and Section III.B uses 'creativity score' for the Total Creativity test (6.03 vs 4.71). The paper never uses the word 'primary', and it later calls all three scores 'dependent variables' and 'dimensions of creativity' (Table II title). Codebook rule 2 would pick this outcome in any case.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O2 was coded as novelty and interpreted as a novelty loss through an inferred sign reversal, although the paper only defines similarity to Earth creatures.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Changed S1-O2.construct from novelty to other. Removed the inferred novelty loss and creativity sign reversal from measure_detail and the reported contrast, and revised the corresponding open question. Retained treatment_higher on the printed similarity scale and every printed statistic. Criterion 3 remains met by the independent coders' ratings of overall creativity and atypical features.
challenge_resolution.quote: Similarity to Earth Creatures: Measured using two items: Similarity to humans, Similarity to other Earth animals. Responses were recorded on a 7-point scale.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 663), Section II.C Experimental Scoring Criteria; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 664), Section III.B and Table II

open_items.item: Randomization procedure and separate testing sessions/settings, including the age imbalance in Table I (open_questions[0]; PDF pp. 2-3). This bears on verification of criterion 1; the explicit random-assignment statement supports met. Author allocation and session records would settle implementation.

Contradictory narrative arm labels (open_questions[1]; PDF p. 4, Section III.B). Table II supplies the coded Yes/No attribution; corrected wording would settle the discrepancy. This concerns effect direction, not an eligibility criterion.

Meaning and aggregation of the similarity score, and the atypical-feature response scale (open_questions[2]; PDF pp. 3-4). The scoring rubric would settle these questions. Overall creativity already meets criterion 3; S1-O2 is coded other without an inferred novelty sign.

Internally inconsistent degrees of freedom, test statistics and p-values (open_questions[3]; PDF pp. 2-4). Corrected analyses or underlying data from the authors would settle statistical extraction; the discrepancies do not change the stated assignment, participant counts or output scoring.

Kimi.AI prompts, generated content and drawing medium (open_questions[4]; PDF pp. 2-3). The task protocol would settle intervention details; the paper already specifies generative-AI access and participant-produced drawings.

Prior-AI-experience category labels and inconsistent control-column counts (open_questions[5]; PDF p. 3, Table I). Corrected demographic records would settle these errors; independent sample-size evidence in Tables I-II meets criterion 2.
Two versus three baseline AUT raters (open_questions[6]; PDF p. 3, Section II.C). Author confirmation would settle this baseline-only inconsistency; it does not affect the eligible drawing outcomes.
